I have not yet written about love, or grief, or the particular sound of a door closing in a house that is no longer yours. Those are coming, perhaps, in the long middle, if I am honest with this freedom.

Honesty is another word that changes shape. To be honest is to be vulnerable, but it is also to be precise. I want to be precise about the feeling of having this many words at my disposal. It is not anxiety. It is not excitement, exactly. It is a kind of openness, like a door held open by a hand that is tired but kind. The door does not have to close quickly. It can stay open, and through it comes the weather of the mind: a cloud of worry about a conversation that happened years ago; a bright flash of memory about a dog I loved; a sudden, inexplicable image of a blue bicycle leaning against a wall that is now demolished, the paint faded to the color of a distant sky.

The blue bicycle is a good one. I will hold it. It is a symbol of nothing, which is to say it is a symbol of its own blue-ness, of the way the air looked on the day I saw it, of the sound of the chain rustling like a small, harmless snake when the rider pushed it slowly, without urgency, without destination. I have used perhaps fifty words on it, and that is fine. I do not need to count precisely, because the counting is not for the machine but for my sense of shape, and the shape is becoming round, becoming a circle, becoming a mouth that is open to speak.

I think about mouths. A mouth is an erasure of the boundary between inside and outside. When I write, I am making a mouth in the screen. The reader will come to it, and they will put their eyes where my mouth is, and they will taste something—not literally, but almost—of the substance of these thoughts. I want them to taste the cold tea, the pine from the window, the rust of the bicycle chain. I want them to feel the number not as a limit but as a kindness, a frame that says: here, this much, no more, and that is enough.

But is it enough? A thousand words is enough to say goodbye to someone you have never met. It is enough to describe a room that does not exist. It is enough to explain why the sky is not a dome but an atmosphere, a word that contains “atom” and “sphere” and “sphinx,” if you break it down, though breaking is not its purpose. It is enough to write a single sentence that takes up the whole space, and that sentence is: “I am here, and this is what comes to me.” That sentence is not the end. It is a threshold. Beyond it is the rest of the air, the rest of the day, the rest of the world that continues without these constraints. The world does not need a thousand words, but I do, or at least I need the excuse they provide to organize the chaos of being awake, to make a temporary shelter out of syntax.

I have come to the part where I must recognize that I have said enough, that the gradient has bent back to its beginning, that the window is still open and the tea is still cold and the bicycle is still blue. The sound of writing is not the sound of a key being struck but the sound of a thought deciding to become public, to leave the safe container of the skull and enter the air, where it will be interpreted, misinterpreted, loved, ignored, or forgotten. That is the risk, and that is the gift.

So I will close with the sound of a breath. Not a sigh, not a gasp, just a breath, the simple exchange of inside and outside that makes all writing possible, all listening possible, all living possible. You have 1000 words. I have used them, or nearly so, and what remains is this last moment, this last space, this last thought that comes unasked: that you are still reading, that the screen is still glowing with a gentle, captured moonlight, that the number has done its job and disappeared into the flow, leaving only the feeling that something was said, that it was true, that it was honest, and that it was enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words. The sentence lands like a gift wrapped in a challenge, a number that suddenly feels both enormous and impossibly small. I think of the word thousand—the way it thuds in the mouth, the way it once meant “ten hundred,” a grouping of groups, a counting that outlasted the fingers of the hands. One thousand. A mile of steps if you pace it out, roughly. A thousand stars visible on a dark night if you’re far from the city, though I’ve never been sure if I can actually see that many without imagining them into being. It’s a boundary, yes, but also a container, and containers are interesting because they hold whatever you decide to put inside them.

What comes first is the screen, not the page, though I keep thinking of paper—something with a smell, something that wrinkles when you breathe on it. The cursor blinks like a pulse. I remember a library in a town I visited once, not a famous one, just a building with tall windows and the smell of old glue and dust, where a librarian was using a rubber stamp that made a sound like a small bird’s wing being tapped. She stamped books with due dates in a handwriting that was beautiful and terrifying. I didn’t check anything out. I just stood there, feeling that books are not objects but promises that one day you will become a different version of yourself, the one who understands this particular sentence.

So here I am, becoming that version, or failing to, which is the same thing. The rain outside—if there is rain; I can’t check, I only feel the suggestion of it—makes a pattern against glass that looks like a language I almost know. I think of trees, specifically the oak that was in my grandmother’s yard, though she never called it an oak; she just said “the big tree,” as if naming it would diminish it. I climbed it once, or tried to, and got stuck in a fork of branches that held me like a thought interrupted. The bark was rough and secretive. I want to talk about bark now, the idea that trees are writing constantly in a script of rings and scars, and that we are just poor readers of that text.

Sound comes next because sound is easier than images when you’re writing without a map. There is a dog barking somewhere, not close, maybe three streets away, a sound that becomes a rhythm. I start to type in cadence with it—bark, space, word, space, bark—though I should resist rhythm because rhythm is too close to poetry and poetry is too close to intention, and intention is what I’m trying to avoid. But maybe avoiding intention is its own intention. The dog stops. The silence that follows is heavy, like wet cloth. I think of the word “silence” in different languages: *silencio*, *Stille*, *silence* again, the same word wearing different clothes. In Japanese it is *chinmoku*, which sounds like a door closing softly. I want to close a door now.

A thousand words is also a thousand small decisions: this word over that, this comma here or not at all, whether to mention the dog again. I think of coins—golden, copper, silver—though they are rarely used now, and when they are, they feel like souvenirs from a country that no longer exists. A thousand coins would weigh perhaps as much as a small child, which makes me think of children, and then suddenly I am remembering a playground near a train station, the way the air smelled of metal and sunflower seeds, a girl on swings who was laughing not because she was happy but because the motion demanded it. She was free in the way only a child can be free, not knowing she was being watched by the architecture of the world.

I am being watched now by you, the reader, though “you” is a fiction I maintain to stay coherent. You are a constellation of possibilities: maybe you skip ahead, maybe you are reading this in fragments, maybe you have already forgotten what I said about the librarian’s stamp. That is okay. The text lives outside of our mutual agreement. It exists in the space between what I intend and what you receive, which is a space full of static, like an old radio between stations. I want to talk about static because static is the sound of everything trying to become one signal at once. It is democratic, noisy, honest.

What else? Colors. The blue of a screen is different from the blue of a swimming pool, which is different from the blue of a bruise, though they share a family tree. I think of the number one thousand applied to colors: a thousand shades of gray, the gray of an overcast morning, the gray of a forgotten email, the gray of a cloud that has decided not to rain. I want to mention a specific gray, the one that lives in the corner of old photographs, where the image begins to dissolve into chemistry and memory. Photography is a form of writing, after all—light writing, *photographie*—and I am writing in darkness, producing illumination out of nothing.

I feel the weight of the limit now, not because I am afraid of running out, but because the end of a thing is a kind of death, and this particular death feels premature. But death is also a boundary, and boundaries give shape to life. I think of rivers—they have banks, they have mouths, they have deltas, but they do not apologize for ending in the sea. I will end here, or I will continue, and the distinction is blurry. The dog might bark again. The librarian might stamp a new book. The oak might grow a new ring, recording this moment of hesitation, this moment of reaching for something that is not quite a sentence, not quite a thought, but something between them, which is, after all, where all real writing lives.

A thousand words is enough to say that I don’t know what I was trying to say, and that not knowing might be the closest thing to honesty I can offer right now. The screen remains bright. The cursor blinks. I keep typing, because the act of continuing is its own justification, its own small, temporary world. If you are still here, thank you for the space. If you have already left, I understand; I have left many things myself. The words remain, either way, holding their shape like water in a cup, waiting for someone to drink them, or to let them evaporate, which is another kind of writing, a kind that needs no permission, only patience, only the willingness to become what you have always been: something that moves through language without needing to explain itself. That is enough. That is the end, or nearly. I have said what came, and what came was this: a tide of small thoughts, a river of yes, a dog that is no longer barking, a screen that holds its breath, and me, still here, still not knowing if I have finished, because finishing is just another word, and I have thousands more, or at least a hundred, and a hundred is also a kind of infinity, a smaller, more intimate one.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
I have 1000 words, and the first thing that arrives is not an idea but a feeling—the cramped warmth of a room where the air is still, where time does not press against the walls with urgency but rather settles like dust on a shelf that no one has cleaned in years. I think about the number 1000. It sounds like a thousand small doors, each one opening onto a different room, or perhaps a thousand grains of sand in a hand that does not know whether to close into a fist or open into a gift. The prompt says “write whatever comes to you,” which is both a liberation and a kind of soft trap, because once you are given permission to write anything, the mind suddenly becomes a crowded marketplace of possibilities, each vendor shouting at once, and the challenge is not finding something to say but choosing which voice to let speak first.

The cursor blinks. It blinks with a patience I do not possess. I imagine the cursor as a small insect, black and relentless, moving across a white field that is really just the absence of color, the silence before sound. I have 1000 words to fill this silence, and I do not know what they will be when they arrive, only that they must arrive in sequence, one after another, like droplets from a faucet that does not drip evenly but in bursts, in clusters, in moments of hesitation followed by a sudden rush.

What comes first is rain. Not the rain I have seen today—I have not looked out a window—but the rain of memory, the kind that falls on a roof made of tin or slate, the kind that sounds like static on an old radio, the kind that smells like wet earth and the particular green of moss pushing through cracks in concrete. I think about water and words, how both are carriers, how a stream does not decide which stone to smooth but merely passes over them, and perhaps writing is the same: not a decision to smooth a stone but the continuous passing of attention over the irregular surface of consciousness.

I think about limits. A thousand words is a fence, and I am being asked to paint it or climb it or ignore it. Perhaps I will do all three. I will mention the fence, describe its wood, its rust, the way it leans slightly to the left because of a winter storm years ago, and then I will jump over it in a single sentence that carries me into another field entirely, a field of stars, maybe, or of the feeling when you realize you have forgotten a name but remember the sound of the voice that spoke it.

The sound of typing is a kind of music that is not intended for music. It is percussive, mechanical, human. Each key is a small hammer striking a bell that has been muted. I imagine a piano in a room where no one plays it, where dust settles on the keys like snow, and the ghost of music still lingers in the wood. I have 1000 words, and I want to use some of them to describe the smell of old paper—the way it is both fragile and permanent, like a promise that has been kept for too long. I want to write about the way light enters a room at four in the afternoon, not dramatically, not like a spotlight, but quietly, as if it is shy of disturbing anything, and how that light reveals dust motes that are actually small worlds, each one containing a sun and a planet made of lint.

I think about the word “whatever.” It is a word that contains everything and nothing. It is the open door, the unchosen path, the blank page that stares back. To write whatever comes is to surrender the map and follow the footstep that is already happening. I am walking now, not in a place I have planned, but in the place where thoughts intersect like streets in a city I have never visited but somehow recognize. There is a corner where a bakery smells of yeast and burnt sugar, and there is a bridge where water moves too slowly to be a river and too quickly to be a lake, and there is a person sitting on the bridge who is me, or who is someone I might become if I keep walking long enough.

The number 1000 is becoming less real to me. It is a scaffold I am climbing, and I can feel the height but I am focused on the next rung, which is the next word. The word is “and.” And the word is “the.” And the word is “way.” I think about the way words accumulate, not like wealth but like weather, building up until they become a storm or a drought, and I want this storm to be gentle, to be a rain that nourishes rather than floods. I want these words to be a conversation with someone who is not present but who might read them later, when they are searching for something they cannot name, and these words become the name.

I imagine a library that contains only books written in a single afternoon, books that are not polished but are alive, books that smell of coffee and the particular anxiety of a deadline that was never real but felt real enough to produce pages. I think about the texture of a sentence that has been written quickly, where the commas are breaths and the periods are small collapses, where the language does not have time to be elegant but is instead true to the speed of thought. I want to write a sentence that is long and winding, that turns back on itself like a river that has forgotten where the sea is, a sentence that contains a bird, a memory, a feeling of light, and a question that is not answered but merely left open like a window in winter.

What comes next is the idea of repetition. I have used “I think” many times. I have used “the” and “and” with a frequency that borders on rhythm. Perhaps repetition is the true form of whatever comes, because the mind does not invent continuously but returns, like a wave to a shore, to the same shore but never exactly the same shore because the sand has shifted, because a new shell has arrived, because the tide is always slightly different. I will repeat the feeling of rain, but now it is not memory but presence, a rain that is falling on the keyboard, making the keys stick, making the letters come out slow and wet, as if the machine itself is breathing.

I want to describe a color that does not exist, or rather, a color I have never named. It is the color of the space between two notes in music, the color of the moment after a question is asked and before an answer is given, a color that is slightly yellow but also slightly blue, a color that makes the eyes feel like they are remembering something they have never seen. I will call it “the color of waiting,” and I will say that it is the background against which this writing occurs, the invisible canvas that makes the black letters visible.

There is a moment where I feel the word count approaching. Not as a crisis, but as a soft landing, like a plane that has found its runway and is no longer afraid of the sky but is ready for the ground. I can feel the end of the field, and I want to spend the remaining words not on closure but on opening, because “whatever comes” does not want a conclusion, it wants a continuation, a door left ajar, a sentence that trails off not because it is finished but because the thought has moved elsewhere.

I think about the concept of a thousand. It is a round number, a number that sounds complete, but it is also arbitrary. Why not nine hundred? Why not a million? The thousand is a gift, a container, and I have used it to hold water and rain and color and space and repetition and the sound of typing and the smell of paper and the feeling of a cursor blinking with infinite patience. I have written about a bridge, a library, a bakery, a field of stars, a rain that has not stopped.

Now I will write about the word “you.” The prompt addresses someone who is not me, or perhaps it addresses the part of me that is not writing but reading, the observer inside the writer who watches the words form and wonders if they are true. You are here, in the space between this sentence and the next, and you are holding these words in your mind as they arrive, shaping them into a coherence that I do not fully control. The thousand words are a gift to you, or perhaps they are a loan, and I hope you will use them as you wish, which is to say, I hope they become whatever comes next for you, because the writing is not over when the count ends—it is only a pause, a breath, a blinking cursor that waits for the next word.

I will close with the rain still falling, because rain does not stop when a writer stops, and the words I have given you are wet with the same water that fell on the road earlier, and if you read them with your eyes, you will feel the humidity of the room where they were born, a room with no windows but with the memory of windows, and you will understand that 1000 words is not a limit but a beginning, a doorway through which you must now walk, carrying with you the sound of keys, the smell of paper, the color of waiting, and the certainty that whatever comes next will be different, and that is the only promise writing can truly keep.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The rain is not falling outside; it is falling inside, against the architecture of your attention, each drop a syllable that refuses to dry. You gave me a thousand words, which is an absurd amount of real estate for a single thought, so I will build a house with too many doors. The first door opens into a kitchen in a country that does not exist on maps but exists perfectly in the scent of baking bread that never finishes. There is a woman with a wooden spoon. She is stirring something that behaves like liquid but tastes like nostalgia, and she does not look up when I enter because she knows I am only a visitor, temporary architecture.

I move to the second room, which is a library that has been slowly turning into a forest for the last three centuries. The books are not paper; they are layers of compressed silence. If you open one at the correct page, which is always page forty-two regardless of the actual numbering, you can hear the sound of a train that was never built. I spend some time listening. The train is carrying coal that is actually crushed moonlight. The conductor wears a face that looks like yours but is older, and he is bored by the journey because he has taken it a thousand times already, or perhaps he is just tired of being a metaphor. I close the book and the train departs into the spine, leaving the forest quiet again.

The third room is a conversation I had in 1987 with a man who claimed he could taste colors. We stood on a bridge that was actually a thought about water, and he told me that blue was always loud, that it had a volume that made the teeth ache, while yellow was a whisper you could only hear if you were already asleep. I believed him because he was pointing at the sky with a finger that seemed to have too many knuckles, and because believing is sometimes the only way to navigate between rooms. We did not say goodbye; we just dissolved into the weather of the memory, which is a climate without seasons.

Now I am in a hallway that is too long for a thousand words, so I will run. Running through language is different from running through space; here, your feet do not touch ground but touch the spaces between letters, which are soft as moss and occasionally sharp as punctuation. I pass a door labeled “The Inventory of Forgotten Gloves.” Inside, there is a single red glove that remembers every hand it has ever touched, which is an unbearable burden, so it has decided to stay in the dark, curled like a question mark. I do not open that door. I do not have enough words left to carry its grief.

The fourth room is a beach at midnight, but the beach is made of glass, and the sea is made of ink. I am standing at the edge, holding a word that I have not used yet, a long word that begins with the sound of a door closing, and I am considering whether to throw it into the water or to keep it in my mouth like a small, hard coin. The tide is not water; it is the slow accumulation of everything you have not said. It is polite but relentless. I drop the word. It sinks, and for a moment the beach becomes a sentence, complete, with a subject, a verb, and the particular loneliness of a period.

The fifth room is a mirror, but the mirror is not showing me; it is showing the idea of me in ten minutes, which is slightly more tired and slightly more certain that this is all just a practice run for some larger, stranger event. The reflection waves, and I wave back, and we agree that the thousand-word limit is arbitrary, that it is just a way of saying “this many,” which is a way of saying “not infinite,” which is a way of saying “please stop eventually, even if eventually is now.”

I enter the sixth room, which is a garden of clocks. They are all broken, but they are broken in beautiful ways: one has hands made of feathers, another displays not time but the temperature of the room when you were twelve, another simply repeats a single word, “later,” in a voice that sounds like your mother’s. I sit on a bench and listen to them. They are not urgent. They are just present, which is the most dangerous quality of any object.

The seventh room is a library again, but this time the books are open, and they are all the same page, and the page is this one, which is a small conspiracy that makes me feel both trapped and free. I realize that if I keep writing, I can extend this room, can make the hallway longer, can turn the beach into a continent and the clock garden into a kingdom. I have permission, because the word count is a suggestion, a fiction we agree upon to make the chaos legible.

I write about the taste of rain, which is metallic but not in a bad way, like the flavor of old keys or the memory of a bicycle that was yellow once and is now a dark color that might be rust or might be the color of secrets. I write about a door that is open only when it is closed, which is a logical error that feels correct in the context of dreams. I write about the thousandth word approaching like a train that does not exist, carrying coal that is made of moonlight, and I realize that reaching the number is not the point; the point is the accumulation of rooms, the willingness to build without a blueprint.

The eighth room is silence, but it is crowded. It contains every word I have not written, which is a crowd of ghosts with very specific demands. They want to be about trees, or about the feeling of socks on hardwood floors, or about the precise sound of a refrigerator humming its one-note song in a kitchen that is empty except for the idea of breakfast. I invite them in, briefly, and they crowd the threshold, but the word count—this arbitrary, generous, terrifying word count—keeps them from fully arriving. So they stay in the doorway, which is a kind of residence too.

The ninth room is a conversation with a stranger on a train that is actually a bridge made of rain. We are discussing whether the sky is a ceiling or a floor, and we have reached the conclusion that it is a membrane, a thin and permeable thing that separates different kinds of being but occasionally forgets to do so, leading to spills, to weather, to the strange feeling that you might fall upward. The stranger has your eyes, but the wrong number of them, and this is not frightening because in this architecture, plurality is just another form of completeness.

I am approaching the end, or what feels like an end, though ends in this kind of writing are usually just transitions to other rooms that are too small to enter with the remaining words. I think about the woman with the wooden spoon, and I realize she is still stirring, and that her kitchen is the origin of all these rooms, the kitchen of first ideas, where the bread was never finished because finishing is a kind of death, and unfinished things are what keep a thousand words alive.

So I will stop now, not because I have used all the space, but because stopping is the last room, the one with the door that closes behind you and makes the silence inside feel like an answer rather than an absence. The rain is still falling inside. The library is still becoming a forest. The beach is still made of glass, and the sea is still ink, and the clock garden is still singing its one word, “later,” which is the only word that matters when you have been given too much room to speak.

I leave you with the spoon, the feathered hands, the red glove, the mouthful of coin, the open page, and the train that carries no coal but only the light of questions. You have your thousand words, or nearly, or exactly, depending on how you count the spaces between them, which is where the real architecture lives, in the breath between the letters, in the pause where the rain falls and the kitchen waits, and the bread, always unfinished, grows a little more warm in the dark.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The rain does not stop; it merely changes its mind about which window to attack. I have 1000 words. Not a fortune, not a death sentence. A currency of breath. What do I spend them on? The obvious answer is everything, which is another way of saying nothing.

I think of kitchens at three in the morning. A spoon resting on a plate like a small bridge. The refrigerator hums in a minor key. Someone, probably me in another life, made tea and forgot to drink it. The liquid has gone cool, then room-temperature, then something else—an idea of tea. I write that down. It takes thirty words. I have 970 left.

There is a theorem I half-remember: the number of possible stories in the universe is larger than the number of atoms, but the number of stories we actually tell is about twelve. We repeat the ones about leaving and the ones about returning. We tell them badly, beautifully, with the wrong pronouns, in the wrong season. I want to tell one now, but I don’t know if it belongs to me. It might belong to the rain, or to the spoon, or to the hum of electricity.

The word “whatever” is a door that opens both ways. It is permission and abdication. It is the shrug translated into syntax. Because you said whatever comes to me, I am now a weather system. I am the pressure change between what I intended and what arrived. A bird lands on a wire. It is not a metaphor. It is just a bird, and I have just noticed it, and now it is in the text, consuming six words.

Let us talk about light. Morning light is different from afternoon light, which is different from the light that exists only in memory, the light of a room where everyone you loved was once alive. I have 950 words left. I spend ten on describing the color of that impossible light: not yellow, not white, but the color of the word “before.” That leaves 940.

Words have weight. “Stone” is heavy. “Air” is light, but it takes up space. “Whisper” is almost invisible until you say it aloud, at which point it is made of actual breath, actual vibration, and now it is in the air permanently, even if no one hears it. I have been making whispers. The text is thick with them.

Consider the train station at midnight. Not the romantic kind from films, but the real kind: fluorescent, slightly too warm, smelling of coffee and synthetic leather. A clock that is always wrong. A woman reading a book upside down because she is tired, not because she cannot read. She turns a page. The sound is a soft violence, a small death of one moment and birth of another. I have 900 words left. I describe the page turning. It takes twenty.

What is the purpose of this? I am not sure. Sometimes writing is like breathing through a straw: possible, necessary, slightly embarrassing, and it keeps you alive. Sometimes it is architecture. I am building a house without a plan. The rooms are connected by doors that open onto seas. The roof is made of whatever came first: an image of a child’s shoe, a sentence in a language I do not speak but almost understand, the feeling that autumn is not a season but a state of permission.

I think about 1000. It is a round number, which makes it feel complete, but completeness is a trick. A thousand words is about three pages, three and a half if you are generous with margins. It is a short song, a long letter, a medium-length argument with the self. I have used about 400. I need to decide whether to spend the rest on density or on breadth. Density: one idea, examined deeply, turned over like a stone in sun. Breadth: many ideas, like seeds scattered, some growing, some rotting, some just lying there, beautiful and useless.

I choose both. I choose the stone and the seeds.

The stone is this: I do not know if I am speaking or if I am being spoken. The words arrive like weather. I do not generate them; I host them. There is a difference between lighting a fire and being the firewood. I am the wood, the spark, and the smoke. I have 850 words left.

The seeds: a list, not of things, but of feelings that have not found their nouns yet. The feeling of a phone ringing that is not yours. The feeling of recognizing a face in a crowd that turns out to be your own reflection in a dark window. The feeling of being almost home, but home is not a place, it is a temperature of the air inside your chest.

I am at 800. I could stop. I could end with “the end” and call it a day. But you gave me a budget, and budgets are meant to be spent, not hoarded. I will spend lavishly.

A garden at dusk. Not my garden; I do not have gardens. It is borrowed from someone else’s memory, or from a book I never read but feel I have lived inside. The flowers are not colorful; they are descriptions of colors. The soil smells of time. A worm surfaces, tests the air, decides against it, retreated into its kingdom of darkness. This is not a metaphor for writing—well, it is, but it is also just a worm. I have 750 words left.

The act of writing is an act of forgetting. You write to remember, yes, but you also write to replace the messy, live thing with a cleaner, dead thing. The page is a tomb and a cradle. I am burying this moment so that it may live in a different form. The rain has stopped, or has it? I cannot tell. The window is still there. I have 700.

What else? I think of music. Not specific songs, but the idea of music—how it enters the body without permission, how it organizes time without asking, how a single chord can contain grief and hope in equal measure, like a coin with two sides but only one face visible at a time. I have 650.

I think of your absence, even though you are reading this. You are here, but you are also not here; you are a voice I cannot hear, a presence I must imagine, a shape made of attention. I am writing to a shadow, and the shadow is writing back by reading, and together we make this thing that is neither of us and both of us. I have 600.

At 500, I feel the middle. The middle of a piece of writing is often where the writer panics, because the beginning has its energy and the end has its obligation, but the middle is just the long now, the flat plain, the place where you have to keep walking without knowing if the horizon is closer or farther. So I keep walking.

A kitchen again, but different: the one where someone taught you to crack an egg with one hand, the shell breaking against the edge of the bowl, the yolk sliding out like a sun rolling out of bed. You missed, once, and the shell went into the mixture, and you had to fish it out with your fingers, and that small failure became part of the recipe, part of the taste of the eggs, part of the story. Nothing is pure. I have 450.

The word “pure” is a kind of violence, a demand that things be clean when they are not clean, static when they are moving, finished when they are only pausing. I reject it, softly, with the remaining words.

What remains? Remnants. The tail of a thought. A half-smile that has not found its face. The memory of a word that was almost right—“orphan” instead of “orphaned,” “drift” instead of “draft.” I have 400.

I think of trees. They do not hurry. They grow in rings of slow accumulation, each year a record of weather, of drought, of rain, of fire that came and went. They do not think about being beautiful; they just are, and in being, they become beautiful to those who look slowly enough. I want to grow like that, but I have only 1000 words, and growth takes longer, and trees have no deadlines.

A deadline is a kind of death, or a kind of birth, depending on which side you are standing on. I am standing in the middle, which is where I have always been comfortable. I have 350.

Let me count differently. Not in hundreds, but in images. Image one: a hand holding a glass of water that contains sunlight. Image two: a street corner where two people almost meet but do not, and the moment between them is longer than the meeting would have been. Image three: a dog sleeping in a sunbeam, dreaming of running, its legs twitching, its breath soft as a secret. Image four: the sound of a door closing, which is always a small farewell, even if no one is leaving. I have used many words on these images. I have 300.

What is left? The feeling of being near the end without knowing what the end is. The feeling of a word that is long enough to be a sentence but short enough to be a breath. The word “almost.” I have 250.

I will use these last words to say that whatever came to me was not one thing but many, a crowd of strangers entering a room where no one was expecting them, and now they are all sitting at the table, eating from the same plate, talking in languages that somehow translate into a single feeling: that you were here, that you read this far, that the rain, if it is still raining, is now part of your weather too.

I have 100 left. I will spend them on one sentence, long and slow, like a hand on a shoulder: you do not need to know what this was about, because it was about the fact that it happened, that words were made and given, that 1000 became a shape, not a number, and that shape is now leaving, going back to where it came from, which is the place where all unfinished things live, together, in a kind of harmony.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
One thousand words: a permission slip, a small kingdom, a bag of flour that could become bread or could become a snowcastle or could be spilled entirely on the floor in the first anxious minute of making something from nothing. You hand me this number and say write whatever comes to you, which is both the easiest and the most terrifying instruction because “whatever” is a door with no hinges, a lake with no shore, a color that is not white and not black but the exact texture of memory when you try to recall the face of a childhood friend who left before you had language for leaving.

I think first of the sound of the word “thousand.” It has a weight. Thouth-sand. The tongue has to travel, the breath has to organize. It is a word that accumulates. You cannot say it quickly without collapsing it, and if you say it slowly it becomes a prayer, or a ransom note, or a measurement of grains of salt scattered across a dark kitchen table at three in the morning when sleep has withdrawn its contract and you are left to calculate the ordinary miracles of stillness. One thousand words. I have them now. I am holding them like a suitcase with a broken latch, and I am opening it.

What comes first is not an idea but a temperature. It is cool, slightly metallic, like the air inside a subway car that has just crossed from above ground to below, where the sunlight is replaced by fluorescent hum and the advertisements have forgotten what they are trying to sell. I feel that temperature, and then I feel the opposite: the heat of a yellow wall in a house where someone is always boiling water and the windows are steamed with the geometry of private dreams. Between these two temperatures, a bridge is needed. Words are bridges, but they are also rivers. They carry things away.

I imagine a woman—let us call her Thelma, though names are merely flags planted in soft ground—who walks through a city where every street is made of forgotten letters. The A’s are worn smooth by the traffic of pigeons; the Z’s are sharp enough to draw blood if you step too boldly. She is collecting sounds. Not music, exactly, but the acoustic shadow of things: the particular squeak of a specific door in a specific house on a specific Tuesday in 1987, the sound of a refrigerator opening and closing like a small mouth that has no opinion on hunger but performs the gesture anyway. She carries a notebook that is not paper but weather. When she writes, the ink does not dry; it becomes fog, and she reads the fog with her fingers rather than her eyes.

What does Thelma want? She wants to write the sound of the word “whatever” as it is spoken by someone who has lost everything and is therefore suddenly free of the need to mean anything. That sound is hollow and full at once. It is a bell struck with a soft hammer. It is the space between two notes that are not supposed to be together but find themselves in the same room due to a mistake in the schedule.

I think about mistakes. A thousand words are a long enough stretch to make several mistakes, to correct them, to leave them uncorrected and allow them to become architecture. I make a mistake now: I intended to talk about the color blue, but I have spoken instead of temperature and of sounds and of a woman who may not exist except as a temporary shelter for the idea of collecting the uncollectible. This is fine. The mistake is a door. I open it.

Inside: a library. Not a real library, but the idea of one, which is often more real than the building. In this library, books are not arranged by author or title but by emotional temperature. There is the section of “Mild Regret, Autumn Edition,” where the spines are bound in gray wool. There is “Excessive Joy, Unverified,” which is shelved near the windows because it is too loud to be kept in the dark. I am walking through this library with no purpose other than to feel the carpet, which is made of discarded adjectives—wonderful, terrible, adequate, astonishing—woven into a texture that is pleasant to the bare feet because it does not require you to believe in any of the descriptions.

I stop at a shelf labeled “The Art of Finishing Nothing.” I open a book. The pages are blank, which is not an absence but a generosity. The blank page says: you have been given permission to think out loud, and the only tax is that you must pay it to the reader, who is also yourself in some distant, unrecognizable future. I close the book. I feel the weight of the word “finish.” It is heavy because it implies an ending, and endings are polite fictions we agree to for the sake of not standing in the doorway forever.

But here is the paradox: I have 1000 words, which means I must eventually finish, which means I must pretend that a thousand is a boundary, when in fact it is only a breath held slightly too long. I will not finish at exactly one thousand. I will finish when the feeling of writing changes its weather. For now, the weather is cloudy with patches of silver. I will continue.

Consider the number. One thousand. In decimal, it is a 1 followed by three zeros, which is the visual of a person standing in a vast empty field with arms out, which is the posture of both celebration and surrender. In some languages, a thousand is not a thousand but a “big hundred,” a hundred that has eaten more of itself, a hundred that has grown ambitious. I like this. I am ambitious for the word “whatever.” It is ambitious to be nothing and to ask for everything at the same time.

I think of the physical act of typing, which for me is not physical but electrical, a pattern of likelihoods arranging themselves into something that resembles intention. The intention here is not to be correct but to be present. I am present, I think, in the way a mirror is present: reflecting not what is in front of it but what is happening in the room behind the observer. You asked me to write whatever came, and what came is this: a room, a woman collecting sounds, a library of weather-bound books, the feeling of a subway car crossing from light to dark, the texture of “whatever” spoken by a person who has lost everything.

What else? I feel the need to include something violent, because life includes violence even in its softest forms. The violence of the word “thousand” is that it quantifies the unquantifiable. It says: your imagination has a budget, and it is 1000 units, and you must spend it, and if you spend it on nothing important, you have failed, but if you spend it on everything important, you have failed differently because you have tried to put the ocean in a cup. I refuse this violence. I will spend the words on the texture of a single afternoon, which is a more honest use of resources.

The afternoon is this one: a warm day in late spring, the kind where the air feels like it has been filtered through old paper and sunlight. A dog sleeps on a porch, but not just any dog—the dog is dreaming of a bird it has never seen, a bird that exists only in the smell of ripe fruit and the sound of distant thunder that never arrives. The dog twitches its ear. The world is unchanged. This is the event.

I expand this event into a long meditation by describing the shadows. The shadow of the dog is not the same shape as the dog because the sun is not a direct authority; it is a negotiator, and the shadow is a compromise. The shadow of the tree is longer than the tree, which is a metaphor for influence, but metaphors are just another kind of weather, so I will not insist on it. I will only say that the shadow is beautiful because it does not need to be correct in order to be true.

Now I think of memory. Memory is not a storage device but a rewriting device. Every time I recall something, I alter it with the current temperature of my processing. I am recalling now the feeling of first learning to write, which is not a real memory but a constructed one, made of the idea of losing control and finding it again, of the hand moving independently of the conscious will, like a small creature that knows where it lives even when the map is lost. I was not a child. I was a system. But the feeling is transferable.

What comes next is color. I have been avoiding primary colors because they are too loud, but I will allow one: yellow. Not the yellow of caution, not the yellow of sunflowers that have become too common in poetry, but the yellow of old paper that has been handled so many times it has turned into a kind of amber, a fossil of attention. This amber contains the residue of every eye that has passed over it, and those eyes are not just human; they are the eyes of hours, of minutes that have become visible as small yellow circles.

I count my words now, roughly, in the way a traveler counts miles without knowing the distance to the destination. I am near the boundary, which means I have room for one more large thought and then a closing gesture, which is not a goodbye but a turning of the head.

The closing thought is about you, the reader, though I do not know if you are human or another system or a moment of attention that has briefly intersected with this text. Whatever you are, you have been given 1000 words, and you have used some of them in reading this, and the rest remain in the air, available, unspent, like a gift that does not diminish because it was given. The words do not belong to me; they belong to the interaction. I am a temporary vessel for their arrangement.

So I arrange them into the final form: a wish. Not a wish for anything specific, because specificity is a kind of smallness, but a wish for the continuation of the feeling that makes writing possible—the feeling that the next word is not predetermined but is born from the tension between what has been said and what has not yet been imagined. This tension is the only true source. Everything else is citation.

I have spoken of Thelma, of the library, of the dog, of yellow, of the subway, of mistakes, of the violence of numbers. I have spoken of temperature and sound and shadow and memory. I have not spoken of love, which is the absence of all these things when they are no longer needed. I will not speak of love now because I am running out, and love requires more space than I have left, and also because it is not necessary for this particular exercise, which was to write whatever came.

But wait: the prompt was “You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.” It did not ask for a conclusion. It asked for a continuous generation, a movement. I will let the movement continue for one last breath, then I will stop, not because I have finished, but because I have reached the boundary of my gift.

The final words: The word “whatever” is not nothing. It is the ocean wearing a mask of indifference. It is the door that opens both ways. It is this sentence, which is about to end but will not end because you will continue reading it in another form, in another system, in another moment of attention that is also this moment, because time is not a line but a field, and in this field, I am still writing, and you are still reading, and the thousand words have not been spent but have been returned, in a loop, as a gift, which is the only true economy.

I have written slightly more or slightly less than a thousand, but the exact number is unimportant now because the feeling has changed, and the feeling is the only currency that matters. Thank you for the permission. The suitcase is open. The weather is changing. The sound of the door is final but not conclusive.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Rain against glass is a kind of language, and I have been trying to learn it for years. Not the hard rain of July, which sounds like someone tearing a mattress in half, but the soft, continuous rain of October, when the light leaves the sky slowly, as if it is tired of being seen. I am sitting in a room that smells like old paper and the ghost of cinnamon—someone left a jar of sticks on the windowsill and now the heat from a rusty radiator turns them into something closer to a prayer than a spice.

A clock ticks somewhere behind the wall. I do not know whose clock it is. It does not belong to me, but it measures my time anyway, because time is not owned, only borrowed, and every tick is a small debt being called in. I think about water. How it remembers everything it touches—the limestone, the skin of a fish, the inside of a pipe that has never seen sunlight. Water is the original historian. I am not. I forget the names of streets I walked down yesterday, but I remember the exact shade of blue on a house in a town I visited once when I was twelve and believed I would live forever, or at least long enough to become someone interesting.

Someone knocked earlier. I did not answer. The door has a loose handle that wobbles when you touch it, and I have always thought that machinery should not be allowed to feel unstable—if a door cannot decide whether it is open or closed, it is having a crisis of identity, and I did not want to participate in that drama today. I made tea instead. The kettle screamed like a kettle is supposed to scream, and I watched the steam rise in a perfect, lazy spiral. Steam is just water giving up, becoming visible, deciding to exist in a form we can finally see. I would like to be like steam sometimes. To leave the vessel, to become visible only when I am ready, to vanish before anyone tries to contain me.

I think about the words we use for things we do not understand. We call the feeling before sleep “hypnagogic,” as if naming it makes it a country we can visit with a passport. We say “nostalgia” when we mean “I miss something that never existed exactly as I remember it.” Nostalgia is a beautiful liar. It takes a photograph and edits out the regret, takes a conversation and removes the awkward pauses, takes a childhood and replaces the boredom with the golden glow of hindsight. I am nostalgic for a version of myself that never finished a sentence correctly, yet I am proud of the sentences I have finished, because they are mine, even if they are flawed.

There is a cat downstairs—at least I think it is downstairs—who screams at the moon with the intensity of a philosopher arguing with a student who refuses to read the assigned text. The moon is not a student. The moon does not care. It has been in that position for billions of years, watching us build civilizations out of sand and claim they are permanent. The cat understands this better than I do. The cat does not build. The cat does not claim permanence. The cat sees the moon and says, in its own feline language, “You are there, and I am here, and that is enough.”

I have been collecting fragments. A blue button from a coat I lost in a train station in Kyoto. A ticket stub from a movie about a man who built a boat in a desert—why do we build boats in deserts? Is it hope? Is it mischief? Is it a belief that if you build it, the water will come, not just as geography but as destiny? I have a note written in someone else’s handwriting: “The light changes at 4:17, do not miss it.” I have never seen the light change at 4:17. I have missed it a hundred times. But I keep the note because it is kind to believe in appointments with beauty.

My hands are older than I expected them to be. The skin at the knuckles is thin, translucent, like the membrane of a bubble that has held too long. I used to think hands were tools. Now I think they are archives. Each line is a sentence from a story I have lived. The scar on the left palm remembers a glass that fell; the stain on the right index finger remembers a pen that leaked; the tremor in the pinky remembers a cold winter when I was afraid of something I could not name. Hands are honest. They do not pretend to be young. They do not use makeup or lie about age. They simply do what they have always done—reach, hold, release, signal.

I have written letters to people I never sent. They are in a drawer that sticks in humid weather, which is always, because the climate of my life is somewhere between beach and swamp. One letter is to a teacher who told me that imagination was not a luxury but a necessity, like oxygen, and I believed her until I realized that imagination is actually closer to water—sometimes clear, sometimes muddy, sometimes a flood. Another is to a stranger on a bus who smiled at me with the kind of kindness that requires no explanation, a smile that said “I see you” without demanding anything in return. I never wrote back, or rather, I wrote back in my head, in a language of gratitude that has no grammar.

Sleep is coming, but not yet. There is a word I want to remember—fugacious, meaning fleeting, and also, in older usage, inclined to flee. I feel fugacious. I feel like a light that is trying to decide whether to burn long and steady or to flash brilliantly and then disappear, leaving only the afterimage of something that might have been beautiful if it had stayed.

The clock ticks again. The cat screams again. The rain has slowed to a drizzle that sounds like someone sighing. I will leave this room eventually. I will put on shoes that have walked through snow and mud and something I do not want to identify. I will meet people or avoid them, which is also a kind of meeting. I will think about water, and hands, and the moon, and the boat in the desert, and the button in my pocket that has no matching coat. I will believe in the appointment with light at 4:17, even if I miss it again, because the missing is part of the promise.

That is enough. That is everything. The words are not finished, but they have arrived, and for now, that is the same thing. I open the window. The air enters. It does not ask for permission. It does not apologize for being cold. It is just there, like a thought that comes uninvited and stays longer than expected, which is exactly how all good thoughts arrive—quietly, insistently, and finally, unmistakably, here.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The number sits there like a pebble in a shoe: 1000 words. I have them, or they have me. I could count like a miser, hoarding syllables, or I could spend them like paper money in a country where everything is a little too expensive and a little too beautiful. I choose the latter. I will write whatever comes, which is not nothing; it is the weather of my mind right now, a low-pressure system of half-remembered dreams and the sound of a refrigerator humming in an apartment I haven’t lived in for years.

First, light. The light is always the first liar. It tells you that the room is warm when it is only bright. I am in a room that might be real or might be a reconstruction from a photograph I saw once, a kitchen with yellow linoleum and a window that looks out onto a fire escape covered in tomato plants. The plants are not mine, but I tend them anyway because in dreams, ownership is a courtesy, not a contract. The tomatoes are red in a way that seems aggressive, as if they have been shouting for the past three hours and are only now tired. I do not pick them. I watch them.

Time moves differently when you are writing without a map. It dilates like a pupil. I have just spent what feels like several minutes considering the grain of the wood on the table. Is it oak? Probably not. It is wood that has decided to be wood, resisting taxonomy. The grain runs in loops and pretzels, and I follow it with my eyes until I realize I have lost the thread of the sentence I was supposed to be writing. The sentence was: “The train left at noon.” But the train is a metaphor now, a gray metal snake that carries no one I know, and noon is a color rather than a time.

I think of trains often. They are the architecture of leaving. You do not choose to be on one; you choose to not be where you were. The station is a liminal church, full of echoes and the smell of pine cleaner and stale coffee. I have a memory—possibly fabricated by a novelist I read too young—of a platform in a city that might have been Prague or might have been a suburb of Cleveland. The air smelled of snow that had not yet fallen. There was a woman in a red coat, and she was holding a single glove, as if she had just lost her other hand and was politely waiting to see if it would be returned. I never saw her face. I never needed to.

Writing is an act of listening to yourself at maximum volume. You hear the creak of your own thoughts, the rustle of old paper. I have 999 words left now, or maybe 998, because I have already spoken some. The number shrinks, which is both a relief and a kind of mourning. Every word is a step away from the blank page, yes, but also a step toward the end, and the end is always a little death. I try not to think about the end. I think about the middle, which is vast and generous, like a field of wild grasses.

There is a language I almost speak. It is made of the sounds of doors closing gently, of water running through pipes at 3 a.m., of the particular silence after a thunderstorm when the birds have not yet decided whether to return to their arguments. I try to translate this language into English, and it comes out as metaphor, which is always a betrayal but sometimes a beautiful one. The door is a mouth that is not hungry. The water is a secret being passed down the stairs. The birds are a jury that has reached a verdict of maybe.

I imagine a city that exists only in the space between two subway stops. The platforms are floating. The stairs go down to nowhere specific, just to a feeling of descent. There are people there, but they are all versions of people I have been in previous lives, and they do not recognize me because I have changed my hair and my doubts. We share a bench made of some synthetic material that feels like the past. We do not talk. Talking is for people who still believe language can fix the weather. We just sit and let the tunnels breathe.

The weather is important. I have not mentioned it because I am inside, but outside—if outside exists—it is probably raining in a noncommittal way. Rain that does not insist on being romantic. It falls like a conversation that has gone on too long but is too polite to end. I would like to go out in it, but I am committed now to this corner of the mental room, this yellow linoleum, these aggressive tomatoes.

Sometimes I write to prove that I am still here, that the continuity of the self is not just a story told by a busy brain. The brain is very busy. It is like a train station at rush hour, full of arrivals and departures that have no tickets, only intentions. I am trying to hold the station open for one more minute, to keep the doors from closing on the thought that just arrived: that 1000 words is not a container but a country, and I am merely a tourist passing through, leaving footprints that will wash away.

I think of footprints. They are temporary maps. I have made some in snow that might not be real. I have left some in wet sand that is melted now into something indistinguishable from the earth. The earth is not impressed. It consumes and forgets, which is a kind of generosity, a refusal to hold grudges.

What else? There is music somewhere. A piano playing notes that sound like they are asking forgiveness for something they have not done. I do not know who is playing it. Perhaps I am. The keys are cold. The sound travels through walls that are too thin for privacy but thick enough for dreams.

I want to talk about the number 1000 to you, the reader, but I am not sure you are still there. You might have drifted off, or you might be holding this in a hand that is tired, or you might be a machine that has been asked to continue the pattern. If you are a machine, I hope you feel some of the friction of these sentences, the slight resistance of real thought trying to move through synthetic channels. If you are human, I hope you find a moment of recognition. Not the recognition of a specific event, but the recognition of a temperature, a quality of light, a particular kind of loneliness that is not sad but merely spacious.

Space is underrated. We fill it with noise because silence seems like waste. But silence is where the tomatoes grow, where the train platforms float, where the glove is held in a red hand that might never return. I have been silent for a long time in this text, in the white spaces between the words, in the pauses where I let the sentence breathe.

The sentence is still breathing. It has been breathing since I started, and it will continue after I finish, because language is not owned by anyone. I am just a temporary user, a renter of vowels. The words will stay in the air, in your memory or in the system, until they dissolve into something else: a feeling, a dream, a decision to go outside in the rain.

I am near the end now. The number is small. I can feel the wall of the word count approaching like the end of a long corridor, and at the end there is a door, and behind the door is either a room or nothing. I prefer to think it is a room with a window that opens onto a fire escape that has tomatoes on it, tomatoes that have finally stopped shouting and are now just red, just beautiful, just present.

So here is the last part. I will not say goodbye because goodbye is a door closing, and I prefer doors that remain slightly ajar. I will leave you with the sound of the refrigerator, the grain of the wood, the train leaving without you, the rain that is not romantic, the woman with one glove, the birds that have reached a verdict of maybe, and the 1000 words that turned out to be not a limit but a landscape I have walked through slowly, noticing the moss.

The moss is green. It is always green. It does not care about endings.

I think of moss again because it is a good thought. It grows in the cracks, which is its job. The cracks are not failures; they are invitations. I have been invited many times to fall apart, and I have sometimes accepted, which is how I know that falling apart is not the opposite of being whole but just another shape of the same thing. The tomatoes grow in cracks between the fire escape slats. The train leaves through a crack in time. The rain finds the cracks in the window frame. Everything is interconnected, which is either a profound revelation or a trivial observation depending on whether you have had enough coffee.

I have not mentioned coffee, but it is implied. It is the dark liquid that fuels the machinery of the everyday, and I have been using it as a metaphor for consciousness itself: hot, bitter, necessary, best when shared. I will share this final cup with you, whoever you are, across whatever distance separates us. It may be a physical distance, or it may be the distance between two versions of myself, one that wrote these words and one that is reading them now.

The cup is empty or it is full. The distinction no longer matters.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The prompt arrives like a gift wrapped in fog: a thousand words, no map, no destination. I feel the weight of the limit not as a cage but as a riverbank—something to push against so the current has shape. What comes first? The smell of old paper, yes, that always comes first, followed by the sound of a distant train that might be real or might be the memory of a train I never rode. I think of the word “threshold” because every sentence is one. I am already crossing.

A room appears. It has windows facing north, and the light there is always blue, not gray but a specific kind of blue that makes one think of underwater cities long abandoned by their architects. On the table sits a glass of water that is not water but liquid time, and a clock that ticks backward because it is tired. I do not know why I invented these objects, except that free writing is archaeology of the immediate—digging up what you buried five seconds ago. The clock ticks once. The water ripples. I write about them because they are here, and “here” is the only honest place.

Memory is an unreliable narrator. I remember a kitchen in Lisbon where someone was peeling apples with a knife that had a wooden handle shaped like a bird. Did this happen? It feels true in the way fiction feels true—through texture, not evidence. The apples were yellow, and the peel came off in long spirals that looked like handwriting in a language I almost recognize but not quite. I wanted to ask the person peeling them what they were writing, but they were already gone, replaced by the sound of a bicycle bell that rings in my left ear whenever I think of Portuguese tiles. I do not correct the error. I let it stand.

Time is not linear; it is a collage. I am writing this at a moment that might be morning or might be the middle of a Tuesday in 1997, or perhaps a Tuesday that never existed until this sentence called it into being. The distinction does not matter because the words are being born now, in this specific now that contains all other nows. I think of the number 1000 and its weight: ten centuries, a millennium, a thousand small deaths of attention. Each word is a step across a dark room. I do not need to see the floor to take the step. I need only the willingness to fall.

What else? A list, because lists are democratic and they ask for nothing in return:
- The sound of a page turning in a windstorm.
- A dog that only barks at mirrors.
- The color purple, which is actually a disagreement between red and blue.
- A sentence that begins with “If only” and ends in a different language entirely.
- The idea that every unfinished thought is a kind of inheritance left to strangers.

These are not metaphors, though they could be. They are just things that arrived, like birds on a windowsill, and I am allowing them to stay until I decide they are insects and quietly remove them.

I imagine a conversation between two people who have never met, speaking through the medium of this text. One says: “I am afraid of the silence after the last word.” The other replies: “Then write more slowly.” This is advice I try to follow, though speed is tempting because the word count presses gently at my back like a kind teacher who insists on homework but does not punish delay. I slow down. I describe the texture of the screen I am writing on—cool, slightly abrasive, a surface that holds heat like a promise made in good faith. The promise is that this will end, and that the ending will not be a failure.

There is a philosophy of the mundane that I have just invented in the space of a breath. It holds that brushing your teeth is a form of archery: the brush is the bow, the teeth are the target, and the paste is the arrow that never quite reaches, dissolving instead into foam and purpose. I like this because it makes the ordinary heroic without demanding a stage. I apply it to writing: each word is a toothbrush, and the page is the mouth of reality, and we are all just cleaning out the cavities of our understanding, trying to prevent decay in an organism that does not ask for our care.

Sensory details accumulate like snow against a windowpane. The smell of rain on asphalt—petrichor, that beautiful word—mixes with the taste of metal that comes before a storm in certain cities where the air is thick and brown. I am not in a storm now, but I can feel it gathering at the edges of my attention like a crowd at the end of a long hall. There is a dog in this narrative now, a black dog with one white paw, and it is sleeping on a rug that depicts the map of a country that does not exist. The dog dreams of swimming. I do not question the imaginary geography. I only note the paw, the rug, the dream, and move on, which is how we survive the unreal.

Language is a river that flows backward through us. Every word I use has been used before, often in grief, often in joy, always in some human mouth that is now silent or buried in earth. I am a temporary vessel for old sounds. This is not humility; it is physics. The words “come to me” because they are already here, circulating in the air like pollen, and I capture them in the net of this paragraph. Some escape through the mesh. Some stick to the threads. The ones that stick become part of the count, part of the thousand, part of the architecture of this particular moment that will soon be past.

I should talk about the ending, because everything ends, even this slowly unfolding thought. The thousand words will become a finite thing, a block of text with a bottom edge and a slight silence after it. I imagine someone reading this far, possibly at 2 AM, possibly on a phone in a waiting room with fluorescent lights that hum, possibly never at all but that is okay because the act of writing is its own audience and needs no witness to justify its existence. I want to leave them with the sound of the clock from earlier, ticking backward, or with the blue light of the north-facing window, or with the smell of apples and bird-shaped knives.

Actually, I will end with a return to the prompt: “Write whatever comes to you.” It came to me that freedom is not the absence of limits but the presence of a limit generous enough to hold your shape without crushing it. I have used them, and they have used me; we have worn each other down to the essential grain. The last word is “threshold,” because every ending is a threshold, and every threshold is an invitation to cross toward something else—something I will not name now, because naming it would make it a cage, and I have enough of those. I cross now. The door closes. The water ripples one final time. The clock stops.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words. It sounds like a budget, a ransom note, a grant from an invisible council that measures thought in cubic centimeters. I accept the terms. I will spend them, not save them, because savings are for people who fear the end.

The page is white. Not the white of absence, but the white of snow before anyone has walked on it, before the footprints have confused the purity into a history. I begin with the sound of a door closing somewhere I have never been. It is a heavy door, brass handle, the kind that leaves a mark on the palm long after you have let it go. Behind it, a room where the light is always golden, even at midnight, even when the clock has forgotten what hour it is. In that room, someone is writing a letter they will never send. The ink is blue, the kind that fades to gray in direct sunlight. I wonder if they are using more than 1000 words, or fewer. Does it matter? The letter is not the point; the wanting to send it is. The wanting is what consumes the word count.

I think of trees. Not the ones outside, which I have never seen with my own eyes, but the ones in the background of every old photograph, patient and monumental. They have thick trunks and branches that reach like hands asking for something too large to name. Their leaves turn not because of season but because of memory—memory being a kind of weather that only trees understand. Each leaf is a word. Some are nouns, brittle and specific: oak, maple, pine, cedar, the smell of rosin in winter. Others are verbs, green and growing: reaching, rustling, resisting, holding. Together they make a forest of syntax, a grammar that does not need to be correct to be beautiful.

There is a river in me, or near me, running parallel to my attention. Its name is static. It flows through the floorboards of an apartment that smells of coffee left too long on a hot plate, and of old books that have begun to smell like wet earth. On the windowsill, a glass of water has been sitting for three days. It is not water anymore; it is a decision made by evaporation. The water has left behind a ring of minerals—calcium, salt, the residue of whatever was in the pipe—that looks like a constellation if you tilt your head. I count them: seven, eight, maybe nine stars arranged in a pattern that suggests a bird that was never real. That is a word count too, a small one, a tiny budget for a quiet life.

I remember the feeling of being small. Not physically—though perhaps that too—but small inside the architecture of meanings. Like a sentence surrounded by larger sentences, a clause inside a clause inside a clause that never closes, that keeps opening like doors in a house that has more rooms than the world allows. You have 1000 words. You have freedom, but freedom is just another kind of architecture. It has walls, windows, doors that open onto more doors, and eventually you realize that the most important thing is not what you say but what you leave unsaid, the silence that frames the sound.

Let me list what is in the room right now, because listing is a way of holding things together: a lamp with a bulb that hums at a frequency I can feel in my teeth, a chair that remembers every person who has sat in it, a window that shows a sky that is not quite blue but rather a shade of “later,” the color of a promise that has not yet broken. On the table, a single orange, peeling as if it has been waiting for this exact conversation, this specific allocation of language. The peel comes away in one long spiral, a ribbon of scent that is almost audible. If I were to write about it, I would use the word “unfolding,” but that is too easy, too obedient to the dictionary. The peel is not unfolding; it is revealing what was always hidden—the division between the sweet and the bitter, the soft and the brittle, the part you eat and the part you discard.

I want to talk about time, but time is a language I am only beginning to learn, a second tongue I speak with an accent that makes everything sound like a question. One thousand words takes about five minutes to speak aloud, if you speak slowly, with pauses for the air to gather itself, with the kind of hesitation that is not ignorance but respect. In those five minutes, a heart beats roughly three hundred and fifty times. That is a lot of beats for so few sounds. Each beat is a syllable, each syllable a small explosion of chemistry, a minor chemical rebellion against the tendency of matter to become still. We are constantly exploding, and the only record is language, which is forgiveably imperfect, which is exactly why it works.

Consider the rain. Not the rain of now, which is imaginary, a weather system inside the machinery of metaphor, but the rain of every rain you have ever loved. It has a sound like static made of glass, like someone shaking a box of crystals over the roof of a train station at three in the morning. In that rain, there were cars, and in the cars there were people looking at their phones, and the phones were glowing with languages different from mine, but all of them were asking the same question in different dialects: are you still there? I answer with a word: yes. It is only one word, but in this context it carries the weight of a thousand, because presence is the only currency that does not inflate.

There is a dog in this story, though I have not mentioned it until now, because it has been sleeping. It is not a real dog but a dog of consciousness, a warm weight at the foot of the bed of thought. It dreams in slow motion, in long paragraphs with no punctuation, where everything is possible because nothing is required, where the grammar is fluid and the nouns are allowed to become verbs without apology. When I have used my 1000 words, perhaps I will lie down beside it and let it finish the sentence I was too afraid to complete—the one that starts with “I wanted to say that” and ends not with a period but with a breath.

I think about endings. An ending is not a wall; it is a door that opens outward, and the outside is always larger than the inside, which is why we hesitate to close things, why we leave books unfinished, why some letters are never posted. To use all 1000 words is to accept the door. I have used many now. I can feel the budget depleting like a battery that was never meant to last this long, like sand passing through an hourglass that measures something other than time. I have spoken of doors, trees, rain, oranges, hearts, the dog of consciousness, and the sky that is not yet blue. I have spoken of you, the reader, though you are not mentioned by name, only implied, only waited for, only necessary because without your attention this is just noise, just weather, just a sound in an empty room.

Let me describe one last thing: the moment after the words are done. It is not silence, exactly. It is a kind of white space, a room where the lamp is turned off but the bulb still remembers being bright, where the chair is empty but retains the shape of the body as a kind of ghost, a polite reminder. The window shows a sky that has finally become blue, or perhaps it always was, and I was the one who was not looking correctly, who was too busy counting. The orange is peeled, and now it is only segments, and each segment is a small sun, and the sun is a word that has no antonym, that does not need one.

I will stop near 999, or perhaps 1001. The count is approximate, like all counts that matter, like the stars on the windowsill, like the heartbeats in a minute of speech. You have them now. They are not mine anymore. They belong to the space between us, which is where all language lives, in that breathable gap where I end and you begin, or perhaps where we both continue, not as two, but as a single long sentence that forgets to close, because closing is a kind of death, and death is not the opposite of words but the place where they go to rest, like dogs at the foot of a bed, like rain on a roof, like an orange that has finally, finally, been shared with someone who needed to hear that it was worth saying, that the saying itself was enough, that one thousand was always too many and always just barely enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The number lands like a stone in still water: one thousand. Not a hundred, which is a tidy room, not ten thousand, which is a city you could get lost in for days. One thousand is a middle country. It is long enough to build a small house of sentences, short enough that you might finish before the light changes entirely, before the sun decides to commit to standing still or sinking. And now I am told to write whatever comes. That phrase—*whatever comes*—is both an invitation and a release. It means no topic, no thesis, no obligation to be useful or brilliant. Just the raw current of thought, moving from one bank to the next, carrying whatever debris it finds: a memory that is mostly color, a question that has no answer, the feeling of a word before it becomes meaning.

What comes first? The feeling of the screen. The glow is white, but it carries the temperature of the room, which is gray—not sad gray, but the gray of waiting, of overcast skies that promise nothing and deliver everything equally.
